title: Hamming vs Cekura 2026: How They Differ on Pricing and AI Judge Checks
summary: Hamming vs Cekura: Cekura publishes metered prices, Hamming quotes every plan, and each checks its AI judge differently. Compare current plans and prices.
body_markdown:
If Hamming and Cekura are both on your shortlist, you’re looking at two young voice agent testing tools that do much of the same job. Both run simulated calls against your agent, score calls with an AI judge (a language model that grades the conversation against criteria you set), monitor production calls, and help turn failures into new tests. So Hamming vs Cekura comes down to two things: how you buy each one, and how each one checks the judge behind its scores.


Cekura publishes prices for two of its three plans, Pay as you go and Startup; Enterprise is custom. You start on free credits with no card, and on the pay-as-you-go plan, each seat after the first costs $30 a month. Hamming sells through a sales call: neither of its two plans lists a price. On scores, Hamming leads with how accurate its judge is, and a reviewer checks the calls the judge flags. Cekura sends ambiguous calls to a person, who can override the judge.


Below, we cover what Hamming and Cekura share, how you buy each, and how each checks its judge, then what a regulated team needs that neither difference settles.


Here’s how the two compare, based on each vendor’s pricing and FAQ pages as of November 2026.

## Hamming and Cekura run the same testing loop


Line up the feature lists and the two are hard to tell apart. Both test chat agents as well as voice, and a call that fails in production can become a regression test that reruns on later releases.


The enterprise basics match too. Both cover SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA, offer self-hosting to enterprise customers on request, connect through an API, and run in CI. And both are seed-stage companies. With that much in common, the choice comes down to how you buy and whether you can trust the scores.


## Hamming vs Cekura pricing: published rates vs a sales call


The first difference shows up on the pricing pages.[Cekura’s](https://www.cekura.ai/pricing) opens at $0 with “No card required.”[Hamming’s](https://hamming.ai/pricing) lists two plans, Production and Enterprise, with no prices and a “Request a demo” button on each.


Cekura’s pay-as-you-go plan charges $0.25 per minute of simulated voice testing and $0.05 for each production call it monitors. You start with 300 free credits, which Cekura puts at about 60 minutes of testing. On that plan, the first seat is free, and each one after it costs $30 a month. The Startup plan is $500 a month with 10 seats included, and Enterprise is custom. Cekura’s[docs](https://docs.cekura.ai/) are public.


Hamming prices by quote. Its[FAQ](https://hamming.ai/faqs) says pricing is “primarily based on test volume rather than per-seat,” and you can add your whole team without user fees. The same page says, “We don’t offer a traditional free trial with self-serve access,” and Hamming’s[documentation](https://docs.hamming.ai/) asks for an access code before you can read it.


On Cekura’s pay-as-you-go plan, the bill moves with three meters: test minutes, monitored calls, and headcount. A five-person team, reviewers included, pays $120 a month in seats before it runs a single test. With Hamming, you can’t see a price before that sales call, and the docs open to customers after onboarding.


## How they check the AI judge: Hamming leads with accuracy, Cekura sends ambiguous calls to a person


Price decides what you pay. The judge decides whether the results are worth paying for. Both tools grade conversations with an AI judge, so a release that ships on a clean test run is only as safe as that judge.


The difference is which calls a person sees. Hamming leads with its judge’s accuracy, and a reviewer checks the calls the judge flags, using a scorecard. Cekura sends ambiguous calls to a person, who can override the judge’s verdict.


Whichever approach you’re weighing, ask one question before trusting the scores: how many real failures does the judge catch? Agreement, how often the judge and your reviewers give the same answer, sounds like the right measure, but it can hide a judge that catches nothing. A simple example shows how. If reviewers mark 95 of 100 calls as successful, a judge that passes all 100 agrees with them 95% of the time and still misses all five failures.


The number that exposes it is catch rate: the share of the failures your reviewers found that the judge also flagged. Ask for it on your own agent’s calls, measured against your own reviewers.

Human review sits at the center: people review the calls your rules flag, not every call. Your QA or compliance team works in a[no-code review interface](https://www.coval.ai/products/human-review/) built for QA analysts and compliance reviewers, not just engineers. Each[review project](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/human-review) groups the calls to review, the metrics to label, and the people assigned to the work. Auto-add rules pull in new calls whose results match conditions you set, such as every call that failed a compliance check. Failures, edge cases, and low-confidence calls go to the top of the queue. Seats are unlimited, so the whole QA team can review without raising the bill. If you don’t have in-house QA, Coval’s own trained reviewers can label your calls and calibrate your metrics for you.


Coval then measures the judge against your reviewers. For each binary metric, a yes-or-no check such as “did the agent say it’s an AI?”, it reports[agreement and catch rate](https://docs.coval.ai/concepts/metrics/human-review/insights) on the calls your team has labeled. The calls where the judge and your reviewers disagree show you what to fix. In one[published case](https://www.coval.ai/blog/how-to-create-ai-judge-metrics-you-can-trust/) , a team running an outbound voice agent checked its AI-disclosure metric against reviewers on 314 calls: they agreed on 89%, and all 35 disagreements were the same kind of call. In every one, the wrong person had picked up or the caller had hung up early, and the judge had failed the agent for skipping a disclosure the call never reached. One paragraph added to the judge’s prompt fixed it, and those calls came back as passes that matched the human labels.


Every override, annotation, and verdict is tracked, too, so your compliance team has the trail an auditor will ask for.
